paragraphs.text: You are what you eat, or so the saying goes. But Richard Wrangham, an anthropologist at Harvard University in the US, believes that this is true in a more profound sense than the one implied by the old proverb. Dr Wrangham argues that a species can be characterised by its food. And, in Dr Wrangham’s opinion, the fact that human beings usually cook their food is the key to their uniqueness.

Cooking is a widespread human activity. No society today is without it. And eating cooked food in the company of family and friends is normal in every known society. Moreover, without food being cooked, the human brain (which consumes 20–25% of the body’s energy) could not function efficiently. Dr Wrangham thus believes that cooking and humanity came into being at roughly the same time in history.

In fact, Dr Wrangham thinks that cooking and other ways of preparing food provided the basis for the change that underpins all the later changes that made people such unusual animals. Humans became human, as it were, with the emergence 1.8 million years ago of a species called Homo erectus. This species had a skeleton much like modern man’s – a big, brain-filled skull and narrow pelvis and rib cage, with a small gut where food is processed. The predecessor of Homo erectus had a smaller skull (and brain) and a bigger gut, which it needed to process its vegetable-based diet. Homo erectus, however, survived on a meat-based one. The usual explanation for this shift from small skulls and wide pelvises to large skulls and narrow pelvises is the change from a vegetablebased diet to a meat-based one. According to certain widely-believed theories, a reduced gut could support a brain of increased size because meat has more calories than plant matter.

Dr Wrangham disagrees. When you consider the facts, he argues, you find that eating raw meat is still insufficient to explain how Homo erectus managed to evolve its critically large brain. He points out that even modern ‘raw foodists’ (people who are dedicated to eating nothing but raw food), who are members of a city-dwelling, back-to-nature social movement, struggle to maintain their weight. This is despite the fact that they have access to animals and plants that have been specifically bred for human consumption. If pre-agricultural man had been confined to eating raw food, he would have faced certain starvation.

Start cooking, however, and things change radically. It makes digestion easier in three important ways. It causes starch molecules to disintegrate, producing more digestible fragments. It also changes the protein molecules, so that their amino-acid chains unfold and digestive enzymes can attack them more easily. Finally, it physically softens food. Food texture significantly affects the difficulty the body has digesting food. Cooking makes it easier to process, so even though cooked food is no more calorific, the body uses fewer calories dealing with it.

One revealing experiment, conducted on rats, did not involve the actual cooking of food. Instead the researchers fed rats on standard food pellets or on ones that had been ground up and re-compacted to make them softer. The rats fed on the softer ones weighed 30% more after 26 weeks than those fed the exact same number of grams of standard pellets. The difference in the weights of the subjects was because of the difference in the number of calories required for the animals to digest the food. Dr Wrangham believes that the results indicate that the main cause of the modern obesity crisis does not lie in people eating too much, but in the rise of processed foods in people’s diets. These foods are softer because that is what people prefer. Indeed, the nerves from the tongue conveying taste converge in a specific part of the brain with nerves that convey information on how soft the food is. It is only after these two qualities have been compared that the brain assesses how pleasant a mouthful of food actually is.

In support of his thesis, Dr Wrangham has looked at other fields of study and come up with an impressive array of evidence. He cites one study in which cooking increases the percentage of food digested in the stomach and small intestine from 50% to 95%. Previous studies had suggested that raw food was digested equally as well as cooked food, but these studies looked at food matter which had travelled through first the small intestine and then the large intestine. It is true that bacteria in the large intestine do further digest matter, but few nutrients are absorbed from the large intestine.

However, the archaeological evidence for ancient cookery is not as conclusive. Archaeological digs show that both modern humans and earlier species employed fire in a way that almost certainly means they could cook, and did so at least 200,000 years ago. There is even archaeological evidence that cooking took place 400,000 years ago. Older alleged sites are more susceptible to other interpretations, but they do exist, including ones that go back approximately 1.8 million years to the beginning of Homo erectus. And, since unambiguous evidence of cooking is easily wiped out over thousands, if not millions, of years, the lack of strong direct evidence is no surprise. In the absence of such physical proof, Dr Wrangham is instead relying on a compelling chain of logic. And in doing so, he may have cast light not only on what makes us human, but on one of the threats we face today.
